alt: Fresco by Giotto in the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua. Against a deep blue ground, a white marble sanctuary enclosure occupies the left four fifths of the scene, with a canopied ciborium on twisted columns over the altar and a raised pulpit with stairs behind. Inside the enclosure a priest in a red robe leans towards a kneeling youth whose head alone is visible above the parapet. At the right, a second priest in green, seen from behind, pushes away the elderly, haloed Joachim, who clutches a small lamb in his draped arms and steps towards the edge of the platform and the empty blue beyond
caption: The Rejection of Joachim’s Sacrifice, c. 1303–1305, fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), upper register of the south wall. The opening scene of the narrative cycle: the childless Joachim, bearing a lamb for sacrifice, is turned away from the Temple of Jerusalem by the priest, while the offering of another worshipper is accepted within the sanctuary enclosure.

alt: Fresco by Giotto in the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua. Before a rocky ochre ridge crowned with round-headed trees against a deep blue sky, the elderly haloed Joachim enters from the left, wrapped in a rose mantle, his head bowed and hands drawn into his drapery. A small white dog leaps up towards him. Facing him stand two young shepherds, one holding a tall staff, who look at each other rather than at the old man. At the right, a wooden hut with a pyramidal shingled roof shelters a dense flock of sheep pressing out of its dark doorway, led by a ram with curled horns
caption: Joachim among the Shepherds, c. 1303–1305, fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), upper register of the south wall. Expelled from the Temple, Joachim withdraws in shame to his flocks in the wilderness: two shepherds exchange an uncertain glance, while only the small dog springs forward to welcome him.

alt: Fresco by Giotto in the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua. A house shown in cutaway against a deep blue ground: a gabled pediment with a fictive relief of a blessing figure between two angels crowns the main chamber, whose front wall is removed to reveal Anna kneeling in profile in a red gown, hands joined in prayer, a gold halo behind her head. Beside her stands a curtained bed; domestic objects hang on the rear wall. From a window at the upper right an angel with red wings and a halo leans into the room, head and shoulders only, hand raised towards Anna. At the left, under an external staircase with a balustraded landing, a maidservant in pale yellow sits spinning with spindle and distaff.
caption: The Annunciation to St Anne, c. 1303–1305, fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), upper register of the south wall. In the chamber of her house, the praying Anna receives the angel who announces that she will conceive; the heavenly messenger thrusts head and shoulders through the window, while a maidservant sits spinning in the porch below the stairs, unaware of the miracle within.

alt: Fresco by Giotto in the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua. In a rocky ochre landscape against a deep blue sky, the elderly haloed Joachim kneels in profile in a rose mantle, leaning towards a pink masonry altar filled with flames, on whose top lie the skeletal remains of the sacrificed animal. Above the altar a small dark human figure, the soul of the offering, ascends towards a blessing hand emerging from the sky at the upper centre. At the right stands a haloed angel in pale rose, one hand raised towards the altar, the other holding a trefoil-tipped rod against the shoulder. At the left a young shepherd stands praying, hands joined; below, sheep and goats rest and graze on the barren slope
caption: The Sacrifice of Joachim, c. 1303–1305, fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), upper register of the south wall. In the wilderness Joachim offers a burnt sacrifice to know whether his prayers are heard: the victim is consumed on the flaming altar, an angel attends the rite, and from the height of the blue the blessing hand of God appears to accept the offering.

alt: Fresco by Giotto in the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua. In a barren rocky landscape against a deep blue sky, the elderly haloed Joachim sits asleep at the right, completely wrapped in a rose mantle, his head sunk on his knees, before the dark doorway of a wooden hut with a pyramidal roof. From the upper left an angel with red wings and gold halo flies steeply down towards him, right arm extended, a trefoil-tipped rod in the left hand and a trail of cloud behind. At the left stand two shepherds: the hooded one in dark brown looks up and sees the angel, while his companion in a wide-brimmed hat, holding a staff, gazes ahead unaware. Sheep and goats rest on the pale slope between them and the sleeper
caption: The Dream of Joachim, c. 1303–1305, fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), upper register of the south wall. Asleep before the sheepfold, Joachim receives in a dream the angel’s promise: his prayer has been heard, Anna has conceived, and he is to return to her without fear. Two shepherds and the flock attend the apparition from the left, but only the hooded one sees it.

alt: Fresco by Giotto in the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua. Before a pale city gate with two crenellated towers and a round arch gilded on its inner face, the elderly Joachim and Anna embrace on a stone bridge, their haloed heads pressed together in a kiss, her hand cradling his face. Behind Anna stand five women: one wrapped in a dark mantle that half hides her face, the others in festive dresses of cream, red and green, one carrying folded cloths. At the far left a young herdsman with a basket, a pole over his shoulder, enters the scene cut in half by the painted frame. The sky above is deep blue.
caption: The Meeting at the Golden Gate, c. 1303–1305, fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), upper register of the south wall. Obeying the angel’s command, Joachim returns from the wilderness and Anna comes out of Jerusalem to meet him: the spouses embrace and kiss on the bridge before the gilded gate, the moment that medieval tradition read as the immaculate conception of the Virgin. A group of women attends the reunion, one wrapped in a dark mantle; at the left a herdsman of Joachim’s company enters the field, half cut by the frame.

alt: Fresco of the birth of the Virgin Mary. Inside a grey-green house open toward the viewer, Anna, haloed and dressed in red, sits up in a bed with a striped orange coverlet and stretches out both hands to receive the swaddled infant Mary, who is haloed and is offered to her by a standing attendant in a blue and gold dress; a second attendant in red stands behind. In the foreground, below the bed, two seated midwives tend the same haloed infant beside a basin, one washing her, the other preparing cloth. At the left, under the porch of the house, a young woman in cream hands a wrapped bundle through a half-open door to a veiled older woman inside. The pediment of the house bears a carved roundel with a bust flanked by two angels. Deep blue sky above, with losses to the pigment.
caption: The Birth of the Virgin, c. 1303–1305, fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), upper register of the north wall. In the same house where the angel appeared to Anna, the promised child is born: below, two midwives wash the newborn Mary; above, already swaddled, she is handed to her mother, who reaches out from the bed to receive her. At the threshold of the porch a wrapped gift passes from hand to hand.

alt: Fresco of the presentation of the child Mary in the Temple. At the centre, a small haloed girl in a pale cream dress climbs a white external staircase toward a marble enclosure crowned by a canopy on slender columns; a priest in red vestments leans over the parapet with both arms extended to receive her. Behind the girl, her mother Anna, haloed and wrapped in a red mantle, bends forward on the stairs with her hands on the child. At the far left, a figure in a grey tunic, seen from behind, carries a large basket on his shoulder; behind him stand a haloed grey-bearded elder, a dark-bearded man and a veiled woman. Behind the enclosure a group of women’s heads looks on. At the right, seen from behind, a figure in a rose mantle raises a hand in speech beside a man in blue with an ochre hood; behind them rises a tower with arches, an external stair and a pyramidal roof. Deep blue sky with extensive pigment losses.
caption: The Presentation of the Virgin in the Temple, c. 1303–1305, fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), upper register of the north wall. The three-year-old Mary climbs the steps of the Temple toward the priest who bends to receive her, Anna guiding her from behind and Joachim following a bearer who carries the offering on his shoulder. The sanctuary is the same marble enclosure from which Joachim’s sacrifice was driven away at the opening of the cycle: the Temple that expelled the father now opens its arms to the daughter.

alt: Fresco of suitors bringing rods to the Temple. At the right, inside an open sanctuary with a blue starred half-dome, an elderly high priest in a red mantle and white cap stands behind an altar draped in a patterned orange cloth and receives a thin rod from a young man in blue, who stretches it across the altar at arm’s length; a second rod lies on the altar, touched by a white-haired man in a green mantle standing at the far right. Behind the youth in blue a queue of men presses forward from the left — one in grey holding out his rod, others in blue and red carrying theirs upright — and at the very back, at the left edge, stands an older bearded man with a gold halo, dressed in blue and ochre, holding his rod low. Deep blue sky above with heavy pigment losses.
caption: The Bringing of the Rods to the Temple, c. 1303–1305, fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), upper register of the north wall. The unmarried men of the house of David file past the altar of the Temple, each surrendering his rod to the high priest: the rod that flowers will mark Mary’s husband. At the head of the line a young man in blue makes his delivery; at its very end, haloed and hanging back, stands Joseph.

alt: Fresco of men kneeling in prayer before an altar. Inside the open sanctuary of the Temple — a coffered ceiling above, a deep blue half-dome over the apse, from which a pale, worn hand of God descends in blessing toward the altar, smaller blue conches in the side aisles — an altar draped in an orange cloth with a white geometric lattice pattern bears a pyramidal heap of thin rods flanked by two covered pyxes. In the foreground, seen from behind, two large kneeling men — one in an ochre-tan mantle, balding, the other grey-haired in a sweeping red mantle — pray before the altar; at the right, facing them across it, kneels a young man wrapped in a rose-white mantle with hands joined. At the left, a crowd of suitors kneels in close rows, hands folded, their profiles turned toward the altar; at the far left edge a partly visible bearded figure bears a gold halo. Deep blue sky at the upper left with heavy pigment losses.
caption: The Prayer of the Suitors, c. 1303–1305, fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), upper register of the north wall. The rods have been surrendered and lie heaped on the altar between two liturgical vessels; the suitors kneel before the sanctuary and pray for the sign that will single out Mary’s husband. Nothing has yet flowered, but in the blue of the apse, directly above the rods, the hand of God descends in blessing — the same hand that once accepted Joachim’s sacrifice. The panel holds the whole company, and the viewer with it, in the instant between the prayer and its answer.

alt: Fresco of the marriage of the Virgin. At the centre, before the Temple sanctuary with its blue half-dome, an elderly high priest in a red mantle stands between the couple and joins their hands: Joseph, haloed, grey-bearded, in a blue tunic and orange mantle, holds in his left hand a slender rod that has burst into leaf, with a white dove perched on its tip, and with his right hand reaches toward the hand of Mary; she stands in profile, slight and composed, in a pale cream gown, her haloed head bound with a small wreath of leaves. Behind her, at the right, a group of young women in blue, cream and red follows, with a bearded, white-capped elder in green among them. At the left, a young man in a grey mantle raises his right hand behind Joseph’s back, and beyond him a group of young men watches, one in an orange mantle raising a hand while the man beside him lowers a small object toward his knee. Deep blue sky at the upper left with pigment losses.
caption: The Marriage of the Virgin, c. 1303–1305, fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), upper register of the north wall. Before the altar canopy of the Temple the high priest joins the hands of Joseph and Mary: the rod in Joseph’s grasp has flowered, and the dove of the sign perches upon it. Mary’s maidens attend at the right; at the left the defeated suitors look on, one lowering his useless rod toward his knee — the gesture tradition reads as its breaking.

alt: Fresco of a bridal procession moving to the right. At the centre walks the young Mary, haloed, in a pale cream gown whose long train she gathers with one hand, her hair braided; behind her follows a file of young women in olive-green, dark red, black and blue, and behind them more companions. Ahead of Mary walk two bearded men wrapped in rose-red mantles, then a young musician in a pale tunic, his head wreathed in leaves, bowing a round-bodied viella, and two trumpeters blowing long straight trumpets that cross the upper air. At the right rises the corner of a house with a Gothic two-light balcony, from which a large leafy branch spreads over the procession. The background is heavily damaged: the blue survives only in the lower zone, the upper sky largely lost and neutral.
caption: The Wedding Procession, c. 1303–1305, fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), upper register of the north wall. The newly betrothed Mary walks in procession, her companions behind her and musicians at the head — a viella player crowned with leaves and two trumpeters whose instruments cross the sky. From the balcony of the house that receives her, a leafy branch extends over the cortège in greeting. The panel’s upper zone is among the most damaged of the cycle.

alt: Fresco crowning a church arch. In the blue lunette at the top, God the Father, bearded and enthroned within a gold-ground panel with red side-pieces, sits above a marble stepped platform; a standing angel on either side of the throne faces him, receiving his command, and dense ranks of angels in white, rose and gold kneel and hover on either side, a few in flight at the far left. Below, on either side of the arch’s dark opening, stand two identical small buildings with balconies and curtains: in the left one the archangel Gabriel, winged, in pale rose, kneels in profile facing right; in the right one the Virgin Mary, in red, kneels in profile facing left before a small wooden lectern bearing an open book. Richly patterned painted borders with medallion busts frame the whole; the blue ground shows abrasions and losses.
caption: God Sends Gabriel to the Virgin, with the Annunciation, c. 1303–1305, fresco (the figure of God painted on a wooden panel set into the wall), 540 x 845 cm overall. The upper lunette with God enthroned among the angels measures 230 x 690 cm; the two Annunciation compartments, 150 x 195 cm each. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), summit of the chancel arch. Enthroned amid the ranks of the angelic court, God the Father gives Gabriel his mission; below, split across the void of the arch, the mission is accomplished — the angel kneels in his chamber at the left, the Virgin receives the word in hers at the right. The chapel was dedicated to the Virgin of the Annunciation, and this wall is its theological heart.

alt: Fresco of the Visitation. Before a pink marble portico with spiral-fluted columns and an arched doorway, the young Mary, haloed, in a red gown trimmed with gold and with braided hair, stands in profile facing right; the elderly Elizabeth, haloed, wrapped in a gold-ochre mantle over a dark head-covering, bends slightly toward her, grasping her arm, their faces close and eyes meeting. At the left stand two young women, one in pale green with a white mantle, one in blue-grey behind her. At the right, by the portico, a maidservant in a blue and gold patterned gown, her hair bound in a net, stands in profile with hands folded before her. Deep blue background with abrasions; the maidservant’s dress heavily worn.
caption: The Visitation, c. 1303–1305, fresco, 150 x 140 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), chancel arch, right side, beneath the chamber of the Annunciate Virgin. Mary, already carrying the Word announced directly above, embraces the aged Elizabeth before the portico of Zacharias’s house; Elizabeth bends toward her and searches her face, the first human being to recognise the Mother of the Lord. Across the arch, in the matching field, Judas receives the silver — the embrace of charity and the contract of betrayal set face to face over the altar.

alt: Fresco of Judas receiving payment. At the left, Judas, in a yellow-ochre mantle over red, stands in profile facing right, a bulging money-bag hanging from his right hand; behind him a black demon — horns barely visible, a white eye, hooked teeth, clawed hands — grips his shoulder, its dark body almost dissolving into the blue ground. Facing Judas, an elderly high priest in a red mantle and patterned head-covering counts or gestures over the bag with both hands. At the right, two bearded priests in green and grey-violet mantles confer, the elder jerking a thumb back toward Judas; behind them rises a white marble baldachin with carved spandrels and Corinthian colonnettes. Deep blue background; decorated border bands frame the scene.
caption: The Pact of Judas (Judas Receiving Payment for his Betrayal), c. 1303–1305, fresco, 150 x 140 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), chancel arch, left side, beneath the chamber of the announcing Gabriel. Judas, the money-bag already in his fist, settles the price of Christ with the high priest while a black demon grips him by the shoulder; two priests confer at the right. Across the arch, in the matching field, Mary and Elizabeth embrace — the contract of betrayal and the encounter of charity set face to face over the altar.

alt: Two matching frescoed panels imitating small Gothic chapels seen through pointed arches. Each shows a rib-vaulted bay in white, red and blue, carried on slender colonnettes with foliate capitals, opening into a second vaulted bay beyond; at the back wall, a tall two-light Gothic window with a quatrefoil above admits pale blue light. From the centre of each vault an iron lamp — two hoops fitted with candle-prickets — hangs on long cords. The lower walls are revetted in painted panels, grey-brown in the left chapel, veined marble in the right; below each runs a tall dado of white marble framed in dark stone. In the left chapel a small ring hangs on the wall. Above both, a painted cosmatesque border band.
caption: The Coretti (illusionistic chapels), c. 1303–1305, fresco. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), chancel arch, lowest register, flanking the opening of the presbytery beneath the Annunciation. Two painted Gothic chapels, rib-vaulted and empty, each lit by a mullioned window and hung with an iron lamp: no figure, no story, no allegory — only space. Constructed to be seen from a single viewpoint at the centre of the nave, they are the earliest coherent perspectival interiors of Western painting.

alt: Fresco of the Nativity. On a rocky ledge beneath an open timber shed, Mary, haloed, in a mantle whose blue surface has largely fallen away to red, reclines on her side and takes into both arms the swaddled, haloed infant Christ, offered to her by a veiled midwife; mother and child look into each other’s eyes. Below, in the foreground, Joseph, haloed and in a yellow-ochre mantle, sits hunched in sleep. At the left the heads of the ox and the ass rise over the manger. At the right two shepherds in rough cloaks stand with their backs to the viewer, looking up at an angel who dives toward them from the sky; a goat and a small flock of sheep rest at their feet. Above the shed roof, four angels in white, rose and red hover in attitudes of prayer and adoration against a blue ground with heavy pigment losses.
caption: The Nativity (Birth of Christ), c. 1303–1305, fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), middle register of the south wall. Beneath a timber shed built against the rock, Mary, reclining, turns to take the swaddled Child from the midwife, her eyes locked on his; Joseph sleeps in the foreground, the ox and the ass attend the manger, and at the right an angel swoops down to announce the birth to two shepherds seen from behind. Above the roof, four more angels break into adoration.

alt: Fresco of the Adoration of the Magi. At the right, beneath an open timber shed on rocky ground, Mary, haloed, in a red dress and a mantle with extensive blue losses, sits enthroned holding the Christ Child upright on her knee; behind her stand the haloed Joseph and a second angel, and beside her an angel in white holds a tall golden vessel. Before her, the eldest Magus, haloed, in a lilac mantle, kneels and raises the Child’s feet toward his face; his jewelled crown lies on the rock below. At the left stand the two younger Magi, haloed and crowned, in white and orange, one holding a horn-shaped gift, with a young groom behind them gazing up; behind them two camels with red bridles crane forward. In the blue sky above, a comet with a blazing head at the lower right and a long tail trailing up and to the left streaks toward the shed. Heavy azurite losses throughout the blue.
caption: The Adoration of the Magi, c. 1303–1305, fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), middle register of the south wall. The eldest of the Magi has laid his crown on the ground and kneels to lift the Christ Child’s feet to his lips; Mary, enthroned beneath the shed with Joseph behind her, holds the Child upright; an angel bears one of the gifts, the two younger kings wait their turn, and a groom steadies the camels. Overhead, in place of the conventional star, burns a comet — long connected, by a modern hypothesis, with the apparition of Halley’s Comet in 1301.

alt: Fresco of the Presentation in the Temple. At the centre, a white marble ciborium with spiral-fluted columns and a pyramidal roof rises over an altar draped in a red cloth with white geometric lattice; a fleur-de-lis crowns its peak. To its right, the aged Simeon, haloed, white-bearded, wrapped in a white mantle over orange, holds the haloed Christ Child, dressed in an orange-red tunic, who twists in his arms and stretches both hands back toward his mother. Mary, haloed, in an ochre mantle over red, extends both arms to receive him; behind her stand Joseph, haloed, carrying two doves in his draped hands, and a young woman in rose at the far left. At the far right, the elderly prophetess Anna, in an ochre mantle and wimple, raises one hand and holds an inscribed scroll in the other. Above her, an angel dives from the sky toward Simeon. Deep blue ground with heavy losses; dark pavement below.
caption: The Presentation of Christ in the Temple, c. 1303–1305, fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), middle register of the south wall. At the altar ciborium of the Temple, the aged Simeon holds the Christ Child, who twists back toward his mother with outstretched arms; Mary reaches to take him home, Joseph carries the offering of doves, the prophetess Anna raises her scroll, and an angel descends toward Simeon. The Temple is marked by the same spiral-columned ciborium beneath which Mary herself was presented, one register above.

alt: Fresco of the Flight into Egypt, moving to the right. At the centre, Mary, haloed, in a red dress under a pale travelling mantle with blue losses, rides a grey ass in strict profile; the haloed Christ Child sits upright against her, secured by a striped sling knotted over her shoulder, his arm around her neck. A youth with a leafy wreath in his hair leads the ass by the bridle, looking back; ahead walks Joseph, haloed, grey-bearded, in an orange mantle, a staff over his shoulder with a small flask and basket hanging from it. Behind the ass follow three young companions in green, red and grey, in conversation; the youth leading the ass carries a water gourd on a stick. Above right, a haloed angel, hands clasped at the chest, flies toward the travellers. Behind, a steep grey mountain rises to a peak against the blue, with scattered dark trees along its ridges.
caption: The Flight into Egypt, c. 1303–1305, fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), middle register of the south wall. Warned in a dream, Joseph leads his family out of Herod’s reach: Mary rides the ass with the Child bound to her in a travelling sling, a wreathed youth leads the animal, three companions follow, and the angel of the warning flies ahead, urging the party on. Behind them rises the great grey pyramid of rock that makes the journey monumental.

alt: Fresco of the Massacre of the Innocents. At the upper left, the crowned Herod leans from a white two-storey balcony, his right arm extended in command. Below him stand soldiers and courtiers, half-turned away. At the centre, two executioners act: one, hooded in pale yellow, holds a naked infant upside down by the leg; the other, in violet with a dagger at his belt, drives a long, broad-bladed knife while seizing a child a mother in gold-figured blue still clutches to her body. At their feet lies a heap of naked, dead infants. At the right, a dense crowd of mothers presses forward, faces distorted in grief, hands raised, torn or clutching; a man in ochre at the far right turns away with fists to his face. Behind them rises a white octagonal building with two tiers of windows and orange roofs. Deep blue ground with abrasions.
caption: The Massacre of the Innocents, c. 1303–1305, fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), middle register of the south wall. From his balcony Herod extends the arm of command; below, two executioners tear the last child from its mother above a heap of small bodies, while the mothers press together in a wall of grief and the king’s men look away. At the right rises an octagonal building — a baptistery-like structure over the children baptised in their own blood.

alt: Fresco of Christ among the doctors, heavily worn. Inside a deep red hall with an arcaded apse, a half-dome at the centre and garlands hung along the cornice, the young Jesus, haloed, in a red tunic, sits at the midpoint of a long bench, one hand raised with fingers in a counting gesture. To either side sit ten doctors — bearded men in mantles of white, ochre, red and violet, five per side, some gesturing in debate. At the upper left, Mary, haloed, in a blue mantle, stretches both arms toward her son, with the haloed Joseph behind her. The architecture recedes in oblique perspective with arched openings left and right; the painted surface shows extensive abrasion and loss throughout.
caption: Christ among the Doctors (The Dispute in the Temple), c. 1303–1305, fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), middle register of the north wall. In a deep apsed hall, the twelve-year-old Jesus sits at the centre of the assembled doctors, counting his arguments on his fingers, while Mary and Joseph, who have sought him three days, enter at the left with outstretched hands. The panel is the most damaged of the register, its surface worn to the preparatory layers across large areas.

alt: Fresco of the Baptism of Christ. At the centre, Christ, haloed with a cross-inscribed nimbus, stands unclothed in the pale green water of the Jordan, which rises in a mound around his body; his hands are drawn before him. From a rock ledge at the right, John the Baptist, haloed, in a pink mantle over a hair tunic, strides forward and extends his right arm to touch Christ’s head. Behind John stand two men: an elderly bearded one in green and red, haloed, and a young one in blue, without a halo. On the left bank wait four haloed angels in white, rose and pale violet, the foremost holding a red garment over their covered hands. Above, a wide burst of white light breaks through the deep blue sky, and within it appears the half-figure of God the Father, in rose, bending downward with a book in one hand and the other extended toward Christ. Rocky cliffs frame both sides; the blue shows heavy abrasions around the light.
caption: The Baptism of Christ, c. 1303–1305, fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), middle register of the north wall. In the cleft of the Jordan, between two walls of rock, Christ stands in the water as the Baptist bends from the bank to lay a hand on his head; four angels wait at the left holding his garments, two witnesses — a haloed elder and a young man — watch from the right, and above, in a great burst of light that parts the blue, God the Father himself leans out of heaven over his Son.

alt: Fresco of the wedding at Cana, set in a room with high ochre walls, a projecting carved gallery with pierced parapets and vase finials below a strip of blue sky, and striped red hangings behind the table. At the left end of the white-clothed table sits Christ, haloed with a cross-inscribed nimbus, in red and blue, his hand raised in blessing; beside him a young man in patterned dress and a grey-haired haloed man. A girl in pink and a servant in green stand before the table. At its centre, facing out, sits the bride in a red gold-trimmed gown and dark headband; to her left sits Mary, haloed, in a blue mantle with heavy losses, her hand raised in speech. At the right, a stout man in red with a white cap stands drinking from a dark cup, his belly swelling the robe. Behind him a young servant and a serving-girl with braided hair pour and attend. In the right foreground, six large ribbed white stone jars stand on and beside a wooden bench.
caption: The Marriage at Cana, c. 1303–1305, fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), middle register of the north wall. In a festively hung chamber, the wedding feast of Cana at the instant after the first miracle: the servants have filled the great stone jars ranged in the foreground, a serving-girl pours, and the master of the feast — Giotto’s unforgettable stout steward — tilts the cup to his lips and tastes the water become wine. Christ blesses from the head of the table; Mary, who set the miracle in motion, sits opposite among the household.

alt: Fresco of the raising of Lazarus. At the left stands Christ, haloed with a cross-inscribed nimbus, in a red mantle over blue with heavy losses, his right arm extended across the scene toward Lazarus; behind him press four haloed apostles. At the lower centre, two haloed women — Mary and Martha of Bethany — kneel and fall prostrate at Christ’s feet, one stretching her hands to the ground. At the right, before a dark tomb opening cut in the rock, Lazarus stands upright, wholly wrapped in white grave-bandages, his face grey-green with half-open eyes; a man in ochre grips him from one side, and a haloed figure veiled in rose holds the veil across nose and mouth; another veiled figure stands behind. Between Christ and Lazarus a crowd of men in green, red and blue throw up their hands. In the foreground, a man in blue, bent double and seen from behind, and a boy at the far right carry away the great stone slab. A steep rock rises behind the tomb, with two trees on its summit. Deep blue ground with abrasions.
caption: The Raising of Lazarus, c. 1303–1305, fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), middle register of the north wall. Before the opened rock tomb, Christ’s raised hand crosses the panel toward the dead man: Lazarus stands bound in his grave-clothes, grey-faced, his eyes just open, steadied by those beside him, while a bystander draws a veil against the stench of the fourth day. Mary and Martha lie prostrate at Christ’s feet, the crowd breaks into amazement, and two labourers carry off the stone.

alt: Fresco of the entry into Jerusalem. At the left, Christ, haloed with a cross-inscribed nimbus, in a red tunic under a pale gold-figured mantle with blue losses, rides a grey ass in profile to the right, his hand raised in blessing. Behind him follow the apostles, a dense file of haloed bearded men in red, green and patterned white. Ahead, from the right, a crowd streams out of a white city gate flanked by two tall towers: men and women pressing forward, some raising hands, some holding branches. In the lower right foreground, a kneeling man in rose spreads a cloak before the ass; above him a man in green and white pulls his garment over his head. In two trees against the blue, two boys climb and cut leafy branches. Deep blue ground with heavy abrasions, especially at the centre.
caption: The Entry into Jerusalem, c. 1303–1305, fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), middle register of the north wall. Christ rides toward the gate of Jerusalem in blessing, the apostles in file behind him; the crowd pours from the city to meet him, one man spreading his cloak beneath the ass’s hooves and another caught mid-gesture pulling his garment over his head, while two boys climb the trees to cut branches. The white towers of the city wait at the right; between triumph and gate, the register’s penultimate panel.

alt: Fresco of the expulsion of the merchants from the Temple. At the centre, Christ, haloed with a cross-inscribed nimbus, in a red tunic and pale mantle, raises his right fist with a scourge of cords above his head; his left hand grasps his mantle. Before him a trader in violet-grey recoils with raised hand, and a second man in blue and red draws back; at the far right, two grey-bearded priests in gold-trimmed robes confer with others behind them. At the left stand the apostles, haloed, led by two prominent elders; a small child presses into the mantle of one, holding a dove. A red trestle table lies overturned at the centre; at the lower left two oxen move away, at the right a ram stands before an empty wooden cage on the ground. Behind rises the white Temple façade: three gabled porches with rose medallions, marble columns, and sculpted animals — lions and horses — standing on the gable peaks; at the right a carved pulpit-like balcony against the blue.
caption: The Expulsion of the Money-changers from the Temple, c. 1303–1305, fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), middle register of the north wall, last panel of the register. Before the porticoed façade of the Temple, Christ raises the scourge of cords: a table lies overturned, the traders recoil, the freed animals scatter, and a child shelters inside an apostle’s mantle clutching a dove, while two priests confer at the right. In the chapel of a banker’s son, the panel on which money is driven out of the holy place.

alt: Fresco of the Last Supper. Inside an open timber loggia with slender corner colonnettes, pierced Gothic trim, inlaid panels and a red-tiled roof bearing two pale birds and small finials, the twelve apostles sit around a long table with a white cloth, bread and dishes. At the far left corner sits Christ, haloed in gold with a cross; the young John leans on his breast with closed eyes. Along the far side sit six apostles with gold-rimmed dark haloes — among them the grey-haired Peter beside John — conversing in low gestures. On the near bench, seen from behind, sit five more apostles in yellow-white, blue-green, gold-patterned white, rose and grey-green mantles, their haloes rendered as dark discs in front of their hidden faces. The rear wall is pale, with two small windows and faint roundels; deep blue sky above the roof, with losses. A vertical repaired crack runs through the right side of the scene.
caption: The Last Supper, c. 1303–1305, fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), lower register of the south wall, first panel of the Passion cycle. In an open loggia crowned by two birds on the roof, the twelve sit at table in the hush after the terrible sentence — one of you shall betray me: John has sunk onto Christ’s breast, the apostles murmur and search one another, and the five seated with their backs to us wear their haloes dark, seen from behind like everything else in the room. The same chamber will host the Washing of the Feet in the next panel.

alt: Fresco of the washing of the feet, set in the same open loggia as the Last Supper: white pierced trim, inlaid panels, red-tiled roof with two pale birds. The twelve apostles, their haloes dark blue discs, sit on an orange bench around the room or stand. At the centre, Christ, haloed in gold with a cross, kneels in profile to the right in a red tunic, a towel over his shoulder and arm, one hand open and raised, the other at the raised foot of Peter — grey-haired, in an ochre mantle over a blue-spotted robe, seated, who bows his head toward the washing. A dark basin stands on the floor before them. At the left, a seated elder in green and red bends to untie his sandal; beside him a standing young apostle in rose holds a tall red pitcher. At the right, apostles wait, seated and standing behind Peter; a pair of sandals lies on the floor at the lower right. Pale walls with small windows behind; blue sky above the roof with losses.
caption: The Washing of the Feet, c. 1303–1305, fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), lower register of the south wall. In the same loggia where the supper was eaten, Christ kneels with the towel at his waist and washes Peter’s feet; the old apostle, submitting under protest, bows his head over the basin — then wash my hands and my head also. An apostle at the left unties his sandals, another stands ready with the pitcher, and on the roof the two birds of the supper keep their place.

alt: Fresco of the kiss of Judas, a dense night crowd filling the panel. At the centre, Christ, haloed in gold with a cross, in blue and red, stands in profile facing right; Judas, in a voluminous yellow mantle that wraps around Christ’s body, embraces him and lifts his face toward Christ’s, their eyes locked, lips not touching. Around them presses an armed crowd: helmeted soldiers, men in red capes, a soldier in gold-figured armour; above their heads a radiating thicket of staves, axes, halberds and two blazing torches against the deep blue sky, with a white horn blown at the centre right. At the far left, the haloed Peter, cut by the frame, drives a knife toward the ear of a man at the panel’s edge; beside him a hooded figure in grey-violet seen from behind seizes the mantle of a figure slipping away. At the right, a bearded priest in a rose gold-bordered mantle extends a pointing arm toward the central pair. The crowd’s rear ranks are damaged, heads abraded to dark silhouettes.
caption: The Kiss of Judas (The Arrest of Christ), c. 1303–1305, fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), lower register of the south wall. At the centre of the night’s tumult, two faces: Judas, wrapping Christ in the sweep of his yellow mantle, lifts his mouth toward the master who meets his eyes and does not move. Around them the mob’s weapons and torches burst against the sky, a horn brays, Peter’s knife finds the servant’s ear at the left edge, a hooded figure seizes a fleeing cloak, and at the right a priest’s pointing finger directs the whole machine. The dark twin of the Golden Gate: the cycle’s second kiss.

alt: Fresco of Christ before the high priest, set in a night interior: a chamber with a dark coffered wooden ceiling on carved brackets, rose-pink walls with arched doors shut, and a canopied judgment seat at the right. At the centre-left stands Christ, haloed in gold with a cross, in a red tunic and a blue gold-figured mantle with losses, his hands bound before him, his head turned back over his shoulder toward a man at the left whose arm is raised to strike. Around him press guards: a soldier in a red cape over gold-fringed armour, a helmeted man, an elder in blue and gold at the far left with raised hand, a soldier in green-patterned armour gripping Christ’s mantle, and a young man in brown gesturing toward the throne. On the stepped, canopied seat at the right sit two bearded judges: one in red, gesturing toward Christ; beside him Caiaphas in green, tearing his robe open at the chest with both hands. On the upper wall at the centre, the dark plume of a torch flame, its pigment altered. Blue band of night sky above the chamber.
caption: Christ before Caiaphas, c. 1303–1305, fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), lower register of the south wall. The night tribunal: in a torch-lit chamber, Christ stands bound among the guards as a servant’s arm rises to strike him, and Caiaphas, enthroned at the right, tears his robe at the blasphemy — his verdict performed on his own clothing. The panel is among the first night interiors of Western painting, its single torch still legible on the wall though its flame has darkened with time.

alt: Fresco of the mocking of Christ, set in a courtyard hall with slender marble columns, a blue coffered loggia ceiling with gold fleur-de-lis, grey walls with two dark grilled windows and an open door at the right. At the lower left, Christ, haloed in gold with a cross and crowned with thorns, sits wrapped in a gold-figured brocade mantle, a reed in his hands, eyes lowered. Around him: a man in violet-grey pulls his hair and raises a fist; a man in brown-red behind raises an arm to strike; two men in red caps lean in, one stretching a hand to Christ’s cheek; a man in rose extends an open palm toward his face; a kneeling youth in pale blue raises his hands in mock homage. At the centre, a Black man in a white tunic swings a cane back with one raised arm. At the right, a group of standing officials: a bearded man in red with a gold-figured panel, a man in red and white headcloth, and elders in patterned mantles, conferring and gesturing toward the scene. Deep blue band of sky above the loggia.
caption: The Mocking of Christ (Coronation with Thorns), c. 1303–1305, fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), lower register of the south wall, last panel of the wall. Crowned with thorns and wrapped in a gold brocade for a royal robe, Christ sits with closed patience under a rain of blows and parody — hands strike his face, pull his hair, a kneeling youth mimes homage, a stick is raised behind him — while at the right Pilate confers with the priests, the authorities discussing what the room is doing. Among the tormentors, a Black attendant: one of the earliest African figures in Italian painting.

alt: Fresco of Christ carrying the cross, moving to the right. At the left, a city gate with battlemented walls and a pink octagonal tower; from it streams a crowd. At its front edge, Mary, haloed, in a blue mantle with heavy losses over red, presses forward with a hand at her breast, as a man beside her thrusts her back. The crowd follows: men in ochre and rose, elders in patterned headcloths (the surface spotted with dark losses), a young man in a short green tunic reaching forward with a rod toward Christ. At the right of centre, Christ, haloed in gold with a cross, in a red tunic and blue gold-figured mantle with losses, walks to the right bearing the long cross over his left shoulder, both hands gripping it, his head turned back over his shoulder toward his mother. Ahead of him walk two figures seen from behind, one in rose and one in brown; from the brown one’s shoulder rises the faint trace of a lost painted timber. Faint vertical traces of lost spears rise through the pale blue sky; dark losses fleck the crowd’s white headcloths.
caption: The Road to Calvary (Christ Carrying the Cross), c. 1303–1305, fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), lower register of the north wall, first panel. Out of the city gate the procession pours toward the hill: Christ, the great beam on his shoulder, turns his head back toward his mother, who presses after him at the gate and is thrust away by the crowd — the glance between them crossing the whole cortège. He carries the cross himself, as John writes, with no Cyrenian to share it; the escort’s spears rise behind, ghosts now in the damaged sky.

alt: Fresco of the Crucifixion. At the centre, Christ hangs dead on a tall cross against deep blue: head sunk to his right shoulder, cross-inscribed gold halo, body pale and elongated, a translucent white loincloth at his hips, blood running from hands, feet and the wound in his side; above, a tablet with an inscription. The cross stands on a rocky mound at whose base, in a cavity, lie a skull and bone. In the sky, ten small angels in gold, white, green and rose: two at the top flanking the tablet with spread wings, others flying with hands outstretched or tearing their garments, and three holding chalices to the wounds of the hands and side. At the left, a group of haloed mourners: the Virgin in blue, fainting backward into the arms of a woman in gold and the young John in rose; at the foot of the cross kneels Mary Magdalen, red-haired, in rose, her hands at Christ’s feet. At the right, a crowd of soldiers and elders: in front, four men hold and dispute a rose-red robe, one raising his arm, a young soldier in gold-figured armour seen from behind; among them a bearded man with a gold halo looks up at the cross. Spears and a dark banner rise behind, with losses in the blue.
caption: The Crucifixion, c. 1303–1305, fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Padua, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), lower register of the north wall. The cross rises at the exact centre, dividing the world: at the left, the Virgin collapses into the arms of John and the holy women; at the foot, the Magdalen embraces the pierced feet; at the right, the soldiers cast lots for the seamless robe while the haloed centurion confesses. Ten angels storm the sky around the dead Christ, some catching the blood of his wounds in chalices, one tearing open the breast of his garment; beneath the rock of Golgotha lies the skull of Adam.

alt: Fresco by Giotto in the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua. A barren rocky ridge slopes down from upper right to lower left, where the dead Christ lies across his mother’s lap; the Virgin pulls his face close to hers. Two monumental figures seen entirely from behind support the body, Mary Magdalene in red holds the wounded feet, and St John bends over the group with both arms flung out behind him. To the right stand two haloed elders, one carrying a white winding-sheet; to the left the holy women cluster in grief. In the blue sky ten small foreshortened angels wheel and plunge, tearing their cheeks and garments, and a solitary leafless tree crowns the ridge.
caption: The Lamentation (The Mourning of Christ), c. 1303–1305. Fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Scenes from the Passion, lower register, north wall, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), Padua. The dead Christ is mourned by the Virgin, the holy women, St John and the men of the burial at the foot of a rocky slope, beneath ten grieving angels and a single bare tree — the emotional summit of the cycle.

alt: Fresco by Giotto in the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua. At the left, an open sarcophagus of pink-veined marble stands empty; two angels in white and gold sit on its rim, one gesturing toward the vacancy. Below them five soldiers in helmets, armour and patterned brocade sleep in a tangled heap. At the right, Mary Magdalene in her red mantle kneels with both arms outstretched toward the risen Christ, who leans away along the frame’s edge in a white robe, his lowered hand opened in refusal, bearing a tall staff with a white pennon charged with a dark cross and lettered VICTOR MORTIS. Bare stems rise on the hill behind the tomb; green leafing shrubs grow at Christ’s feet under a deep blue sky.
caption: The Resurrection (Noli me tangere), c. 1303–1305. Fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Scenes from the Passion, lower register, north wall, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), Padua. Two angels seated on the empty pink-marble tomb, the watch of soldiers asleep below, and the risen Christ withdrawing from the kneeling Magdalene with the banner of victory — John’s Easter morning compressed into a single field.

alt: Fresco by Giotto in the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua. At the centre Christ ascends in strict profile, wrapped in a white robe within a golden aureole of fine rays, standing on a bank of cloud; his raised hands are cut off by the upper border of the field. Two hovering hosts flank him on clouds — winged angels together with haloed, wingless figures, all with hands lifted toward him. Below, on bare ground, two white-robed winged messengers stand at the centre raising their hands upward; the Virgin in deep blue kneels at the left, and the eleven apostles kneel in two groups to either side, one wrapped in a gold-patterned damask mantle. All faces are turned up toward the rising Christ against the blue.
caption: The Ascension of Christ, c. 1303–1305. Fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Scenes from the Passion, lower register, north wall, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), Padua. Christ rises in profile on a shelf of cloud within a golden radiance, his hands already passing beyond the upper frame, escorted by airborne hosts of angels and blessed souls, while below the two white-clad messengers of Acts address the kneeling Virgin and apostles.

alt: Fresco by Giotto in the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua. A white Gothic pavilion with slender columns, trefoil arches and a marbled base fills the field, drawn in oblique perspective against a blue sky. Inside, the twelve haloed apostles sit on benches around the room: eight face the viewer across the far side, four sit with their backs turned in the foreground, their golden haloes seen from behind. Thin straight red rays of fire descend from above the architrave through the arches, one reaching toward each apostle; the seated men lift their faces and stir their hands. No dove appears — the Spirit arrives as lines of flame alone.
caption: Pentecost (The Descent of the Holy Spirit), c. 1303–1305. Fresco, 200 x 185 cm. Scenes from the Passion, lower register, north wall, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), Padua. The final narrative field of the cycle: the twelve apostles seated in a white Gothic loggia as thin red rays of fire descend upon them through the arcade — the birth of the Church, set at the threshold of the Last Judgment on the west wall.

alt: Grisaille fresco by Giotto in the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua, imitating a marble statue in a niche. A corpulent man stands in profile facing left, bare-legged and barefoot, wearing a crown of upright feathers and a short tunic with ragged dagged hems and a plaited belt hung with small pendants; a long tail of cloth hangs behind him. He raises a knotted club in both hands and gapes upward open-mouthed. The painted niche has a dark speckled ground; the titulus above and the inscription below are largely effaced.
caption: Stultitia (Foolishness), c. 1303–1305. Fresco in grisaille, 120 x 55 cm. Dado of the Vices, north wall, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), Padua. The first of the seven Vices, facing Prudence across the nave: a heavy, feather-crowned fool in a ragged dagged tunic, raising a crude club — folly as the body ungoverned by mind.

alt: Grisaille fresco by Giotto in the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua, imitating sculpture in a marble niche. A young woman in a loose belted gown balances unsteadily on a large disc or wheel that rolls across a steeply tilted floor of red-veined marble. Her body arches backwards, one arm thrown high, the other flung down and back; her gown swings with the motion. Behind her is a dark porphyry-ground panel; the titulus above the niche is entirely lost.
caption: Inconstantia (Inconstancy), c. 1303–1305. Fresco in grisaille, 120 x 55 cm. Dado of the Vices, north wall, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), Padua. The second Vice, opposite Fortitude: a young woman flailing on a rolling wheel, sliding across a tilted floor of veined marble — the only “statue” in the chapel that cannot stand still.

alt: Grisaille fresco by Giotto in the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua, imitating a marble statue in a niche with a dark speckled ground. A heavy-set woman stands with her head thrown back and eyes closed, gripping the neckline of her gown with both hands and wrenching it apart at the breast. Her long hair falls loose down her back in a thick waving strand. The inscription on the plinth below is largely effaced.
caption: Ira (Wrath), c. 1303–1305. Fresco in grisaille, 120 x 55 cm. Dado of the Vices, north wall, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), Padua. The third Vice, opposite Temperance: a woman tearing open her garment at the breast, head thrown back — the gesture Caiaphas performs in the Passion register across the nave, anger made statuary.

alt: Grisaille fresco by Giotto in the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua. A bearded man in a fur-trimmed judge’s cap and ample mantle sits enthroned in profile within the arched gateway of a fortress whose battlements are broken and whose jambs are cracked crags. He holds a tall staff ending in a hook in his right hand and the hilt of a sword in his left. Leafy trees have grown up around and over his throne. In a narrow strip below, small figures enact violence on a road: a riderless horse, armed men, a traveller seized, a woman dragged to the ground, two soldiers with round shields.
caption: Iniustitia (Injustice), c. 1303–1305. Fresco in grisaille, 120 x 60 cm. Dado of the Vices, north wall, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), Padua. The central Vice, opposite Justice: a lordly judge enthroned in a ruined city gate overgrown by forest, hooked staff and sword in hand, while in the predella below his realm travellers are robbed and killed on the road.

alt: Grisaille fresco by Giotto in the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua, imitating a marble statue in a niche with a dark ground. A man in a broad-brimmed helmet and a voluminous mantle stands holding a small female idol upright on his raised right hand; the idol holds a leafy sprig, and a cord runs from her down to a loop around the man’s neck. At the upper right, a half-figure of God leans from the corner with a scroll, unseen by the man, whose helmet shields his eyes. At the lower left rises a tongue of flame. The inscription below is worn, with scattered words legible.
caption: Infidelitas (Infidelity, Unbelief), c. 1303–1305. Fresco in grisaille, 120 x 55 cm. Dado of the Vices, north wall, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), Padua. The fifth Vice, opposite Faith: a helmeted man haltered by a cord to the little idol standing on his own hand, deaf and blind to the figure of God calling him from above.

alt: Grisaille fresco by Giotto in the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua, imitating a statue in a niche with a dark red porphyry ground. An old woman stands in profile facing left, a horn-like peak rising from her headcloth and an enormously enlarged ear exposed. From her open mouth issues a thick serpent that curls back on itself to strike at her forehead between the eyes. Her left hand clutches a drawstring money-bag with hanging fringes; her right hand reaches forward, fingers crooked into a claw. Red flames rise around her from the base of the niche, engulfing the lower part of her gown.
caption: Invidia (Envy), c. 1303–1305. Fresco in grisaille, 120 x 55 cm. Dado of the Vices, north wall, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), Padua. The sixth Vice, opposite Charity: an old woman with a monstrous ear and a serpent issuing from her mouth to strike back at her own brow, clutching a money-bag as flames rise around her legs — the most famous of the seven.

alt: Grisaille fresco by Giotto in the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua, imitating a statue in a niche with a dark speckled ground. A woman hangs by the neck from a horizontal beam that bows under her weight; the cord, painted a secco, survives mainly as a dark vertical trace above her head. Her head slumps to her left shoulder, her arms hang wide with both fists clenched, and her gown falls in long vertical folds to pointed shoes. At the upper left a small winged demon, painted in red, plunges toward her head with hooked claws. Above the niche runs the title DESPERATIO; on the plinth below, lines of the Latin titulus remain partly legible.
caption: Desperatio (Despair), c. 1303–1305. Fresco in grisaille, 120 x 60 cm. Dado of the Vices, north wall, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), Padua. The last of the Vices, opposite Hope and hard against the Last Judgment: a woman hanged from a bending beam, fists clenched, as a small winged demon swoops to seize her soul.

alt: Grisaille fresco by Giotto in the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua, imitating sculpture in a niche. A woman appears half-length behind a tall panelled desk, seated in a chair with ornate scrolled metalwork arms. She is seen in profile facing right, hair bound in a cloth band, setting a pair of compasses to the open book on the desk with her right hand and raising a round convex mirror in her left. The niche ground is dark and speckled.
caption: Prudentia (Prudence), c. 1303–1305. Fresco in grisaille, 120 x 60 cm. Dado of the Virtues, south wall, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), Padua. The first of the seven Virtues, facing Foolishness across the nave: a scholar at her desk, compasses set to the open book and convex mirror raised — the past remembered, the present measured, the future scried — knowledge of the past and foresight of what comes.

alt: Grisaille fresco by Giotto in the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua, imitating a statue in a niche with a dark porphyry ground. A stout woman stands facing right in a mail-sleeved tunic and cuirass, a pelt knotted across her chest and a crested cap on her head. In her right hand she grips a short mace or broken club at her side; with her left she steadies an immense elongated shield, taller than her shoulder, bearing a lion rampant in relief. Five broken shafts of darts and spears remain embedded.
caption: Fortitudo (Fortitude), c. 1303–1305. Fresco in grisaille, 120 x 55 cm. Dado of the Virtues, south wall, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), Padua. The second Virtue, facing Inconstancy: a woman in mail and cuirass, a lion’s pelt knotted at her breast, planted behind a great shield blazoned with a rampant lion and studded with the broken weapons that have failed against it.

alt: Grisaille fresco by Giotto in the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua, imitating a statue in a niche with a dark speckled ground. A woman stands frontally, mantled and veiled, her head slightly inclined with a faint smile. A thin strap runs across her mouth like a horse’s bit, tied back over her cheeks. In her hands she holds a sword still in its scabbard, point down, and winds a cord about the hilt, binding blade and sheath together. The inscription on the plinth below is faint, with scattered lines legible.
caption: Temperantia (Temperance), c. 1303–1305. Fresco in grisaille, 120 x 55 cm. Dado of the Virtues, south wall, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), Padua. The third Virtue, opposite Wrath: a veiled woman wearing a bridle-bit in her own mouth, binding a sheathed sword fast with a cord — force kept, and kept unusable.

alt: Grisaille fresco by Giotto in the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua. A crowned woman sits enthroned and frontal within an elaborate Gothic aedicule with a trefoil arch, pinnacles and panelled sides, against a blue ground — the one blue field among the Virtues’ niches. Her arms extend symmetrically, each hand supporting a shallow pan: on the pan at her right stands a small winged figure bending toward a seated man as if to crown or reward him; on the pan at her left a small winged figure raises a sword over a kneeling man. In a narrow predella strip below, small figures dance in a ring to music beneath trees while riders pass on either side.
caption: Iustitia (Justice), c. 1303–1305. Fresco in grisaille, 120 x 60 cm. Dado of the Virtues, south wall, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), Padua. The central Virtue, facing Injustice: a crowned queen enthroned in an intact Gothic aedicule against a blue ground, a living statuette in each outstretched pan of her balance — one crowning, one striking — and below, a predella of dancers and riders on the safe roads of her realm.

alt: Grisaille fresco by Giotto in the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua, imitating a statue in a niche with a dark ground; two small sculpted busts occupy the upper corners. A woman stands rigidly frontal in a long mantle and a tall pointed cap, holding upright in her right hand a slender staff topped by a cross with a reddish tint, and in her left an unrolled scroll with lines of text. A key hangs at her waist. She stands on bare rock; beneath her feet lie a shattered figurine at the left and torn, overturned books at the right.
caption: Fides (Faith), c. 1303–1305. Fresco in grisaille, 120 x 55 cm. Dado of the Virtues, south wall, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), Padua. The fifth Virtue, facing Infidelity: a frontal, hieratic figure in a pointed cap, cross-staff planted in her right hand, the scroll of the creed unrolled in her left, a key at her belt — standing on the smashed idol and torn books of the old error.

alt: Grisaille fresco by Giotto in the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua, imitating a statue in a niche with a dark ground. A young woman stands turned slightly to the right, looking up, her hair dressed with a crown of flowers from which three small red flames rise — one at either side and one above the crown. In her lowered right hand she balances a wide bowl heaped high with flowers and fruits; her left arm stretches up to the corner of the niche, where a half-figure of God leans down to take the small heart she holds out. Beneath her feet lie sacks and drawstring purses, trodden flat.
caption: Karitas (Charity), c. 1303–1305. Fresco in grisaille, 120 x 55 cm. Dado of the Virtues, south wall, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), Padua. The sixth Virtue, facing Envy: a young woman crowned with flowers, small flames at her head, a bowl heaped with offerings in one hand while the other reaches up to hand her heart to God — her feet on the money-bags she has refused.

alt: Grisaille fresco by Giotto in the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua, imitating a statue in a niche with a dark porphyry ground. A winged young woman rises diagonally in profile, her whole body airborne, feet trailing above the plinth, gown streaming behind her. Both arms stretch up at full length toward the upper right corner, where a small winged half-figure of an angel leans from the frame holding out a crown. Old incised graffiti — small figures and devices scratched by past visitors — are faintly visible in the dark ground behind her. On the plinth below, lines of the Latin titulus remain partly legible.
caption: Spes (Hope), c. 1303–1305. Fresco in grisaille, 120 x 60 cm. Dado of the Virtues, south wall, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), Padua. The last of the Virtues, opposite Despair and beside the Last Judgment: a winged woman rising clean off the earth, arms at full stretch toward the crown held out to her from the corner of heaven — the only figure in the dado in flight.

alt: Fresco by Giotto filling the west wall of the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua, around a real three-lancet window above the door. At the centre Christ sits enthroned within an oval mandorla rimmed with rainbow bands of light, in a rose-red robe, his right hand opened downward in welcome and his left turned away; twelve haloed apostles sit on either side on a long row of thrones. Above them, two dense phalanxes of armed and winged angels fill the upper wall, and at the top corners two figures roll back the sky itself like a scroll, revealing jewelled gates behind at either corner. Four angels sound trumpets, two beneath the window and two beside the mandorla. From below the mandorla a river of fire pours down to the right into Hell, a dark chaos where a huge grey-blue Lucifer devours the damned amid demons, serpents and small tortured figures. On the left, ranks of the blessed and haloed elect rise in ordered processions, with the dead emerging from the earth at the lower edge. At the centre bottom, two angels support a tall cross, beside which a kneeling layman in violet offers a model of the chapel to three haloed figures, assisted by a religious who bears the building on his shoulder.
caption: The Last Judgment, c. 1306. Fresco, c. 1000 x 840 cm. West (counter-façade) wall, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), Padua. The entire inner façade of the chapel, around and above the entrance door and its triple-lancet window: Christ the Judge in a rainbow mandorla between the enthroned apostles and the celestial militias, the elect rising at his right, Hell unrolling from the river of fire at his left, and, at the foot of the great cross, Enrico Scrovegni offering the model of the chapel itself.

alt: Fresco detail by Giotto in the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua. Christ sits enthroned at the centre of an oval mandorla whose rim is built of overlapping scale-like bands — fiery orange-red outside, a white leaf-garland band, blue-green within — against an inner field of golden rays. He wears a rose-red robe with a gold-embroidered neckband; a slit in the fabric at his right side reveals the wound beneath. His bearded face, framed by a radiate golden halo bearing three small dark circular insets, turns toward his right; his right arm extends with the palm opened downward in welcome, the nail wound visible in it and in both bare feet, his left hand turns its back outward in refusal. Dimly visible within the mandorla, the four living creatures flank the throne, the lion, eagle and ox still recognisable. Outside the rim, files of haloed angels press close on either side, and at the lower flanks two angels sound long trumpets aimed downward; at the lower right the river of fire begins.
caption: Christ the Judge in the Mandorla, detail of The Last Judgment, c. 1306. Fresco. West wall, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), Padua. The centre of the Judgment: Christ enthroned within a rainbow-rimmed mandorla of light, his right hand opened to the elect and his left turned away, the side wound shown through a slit in his rose-red robe — and in his halo, the housings of the small convex mirrors discovered in the restoration of 2001–02.

alt: Fresco detail by Giotto in the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua. A young clean-shaven man in a violet-mauve robe and white cap kneels in sharp profile facing right, his right hand touching the façade of a pink scale model of the chapel, his left raised toward three haloed figures standing above it. The first of the three, in cream over red, extends her right hand downward toward him; the second stands between in red with gold embroidery; the third, wrapped in a green and gold brocade mantle, rests a hand on the model's roof. The model shows the chapel's gabled façade with its portal and trifora window, and the long flank pierced by six small lancets and two larger ones. Behind it kneels a tonsured cleric in a white habit, both hands raised to steady the building on his shoulder. Dark blue ground; at the upper left, the wing and drapery of an angel supporting the great cross.
caption: The Dedication of Enrico Scrovegni, detail of The Last Judgment, c. 1306. Fresco. West wall, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), Padua. At the foot of the angel-borne cross, on the side of the blessed: Enrico Scrovegni, in profile and at full sacred scale, kneels to offer the model of this very chapel to three haloed figures, the Virgin among them, while a tonsured cleric bears the building's weight on his shoulder — a donor portrait of unprecedented rank: a lay banker at the centre of a Last Judgment.

alt: Fresco detail by Giotto in the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua. Against a nearly black ground, branches of a broad orange-red river of fire sweep down from the upper left, carrying naked falling figures; grey winged demons seize the damned along its banks. At the centre sits a giant grey-blue horned Lucifer, two serpents issuing from his ears, a soul disappearing into his mouth, another gripped in his fist, while two dragons at his flanks each devour a victim and a figure emerges beneath him. Around him the damned suffer in groups: figures strung up from poles and beams, some hanging by the hair or by hooks, a row suspended from a horizontal bar at the right; at the left, three figures hanged together from a great tree-trunk, a money-bag hanging with them; a pale disembowelled figure in a white garment hangs alone; in the lower corners demons drive and drag crowds of the naked. At the upper left, on firm blue ground, a white-robed angel supports the great cross.
caption: Hell, detail of The Last Judgment, c. 1306. Fresco. West wall, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), Padua. The lower right quadrant of the Judgment as the viewer faces it, at Christ’s left hand: the four branches of the river of fire deliver the damned into a dark chaos where a colossal grey-blue Lucifer devours and voids the souls, demons sort the sinners punishment by punishment — and three usurers hang together from a great tree-trunk, the money-bag hanging beside them — in the chapel a banker built.

alt: Two fresco details by Giotto from the upper corners of the west wall of the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua, mirror images of each other within the curved spandrels of the vault. In each, a haloed angel in a soldier’s fringed cuirass, with dark wings, stands on white cloud and grips the edge of the blue sky, rolling it back in a great curling volute whose inner face is rose-red; behind the retreating sky appears a tall golden door-leaf studded with vertical bands of gems — red and blue stones and rows of pearls. The left angel is seen full-length with booted feet; the right is half-hidden behind the roll, the lower body lost. Above each spandrel runs the chapel’s painted border of acanthus, on red at the left and on blue at the right.
caption: The Angels Rolling Up the Sky, details of The Last Judgment, c. 1306. Fresco. Upper corners, west wall, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), Padua. In the two spandrels at the summit of the Judgment, an armoured angel takes the firmament by its edge and furls it back like a scroll — sicut liber involutus, the heaven of Revelation 6:14 — exposing the red reverse of the sky and, behind it, the gem-studded gates of the city that needs no sun.

alt: Photographs looking straight up at the barrel vault of the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua. A field of intense blue is covered with regular rows of gold eight-pointed stars, bordered by ornamental painted bands with quadrilobe busts and foliage above the uppermost register of scenes; iron tie-rods cross the vault, and grey patches mark losses of the blue. In the centre of the field a round medallion holds the blessing Christ within a feathered rainbow ring, with four smaller prophet medallions at the corners.
caption: The Starry Vault, field of the blessing Redeemer, c. 1303–1306. Fresco. Barrel vault, Scrovegni Chapel (Arena Chapel), Padua. The chapel's ceiling: a barrel of deep ultramarine sown with ranks of gold eight-pointed stars, divided into two fields; this one carries the blessing Redeemer at the centre, attended by four prophets — the painted heaven under which the entire cycle unfolds.

alt: Photographs looking straight up at the barrel vault of the Scrovegni Chapel, Padua. In the centre of the field a round medallion holds the frontal Madonna and Child within a flat gold band, with four smaller prophet medallions at the corners, whose white scrolls flutter out of their roundels into the blue.
